earlier_scan.source_named: Fricke 2019 LOT thesis WAS read (lotpublications.nl): its stress section (3.2.5) describes Central Lembata only, not Ile Ape; only other ref is Keraf 1978 on Lamalera. No description of Ile Ape stress found.

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026 [2025]. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste: Unravelling their prehistory and classification. Berlin: Language Science Press (LSP 526).
sources.note: Only the areal remark (sec. 3.2.1, p. 115): 'While penultimate stress is the normal rule for Wallacean languages, words with penultimate schwa can have stress on other syllables.' Ile Ape occurs only in the classification tree ('Adonara-Ile Ape Lamaholot > Ile Ape Lamaholot [ila] **ʔ > ∅'), footnote 22 (44% lexical similarity with Kedang, Keraf 1978: 448) and the language table (source Keraf 1978). No Ile Ape-specific stress statement.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page ilea1237 Ile Ape (refs: Fricke 2019 pp. 171-228; Grimes & Edwards 2025 pp. 116-122; Eberhard et al. 2025)
sources.note: Bibliographic only; lists no descriptive work beyond the classification references; Glottolog 5.1 export gives Keraf 1978 (wordlist overview) as the sole reference.

sources.citation: Michels, Jos. 2017. A cross-dialectal sketch of Western Lamaholot. Leiden University RMA thesis.
sources.note: Sec. 2.2.1 Stress, p. 25: 'Stress in Lamaholot is not usually contrastive. The general rule is that stress is on the penultimate syllable, but even neighbouring dialects may vary in the details.. Rather less is known about stress in most dialects outside of Flores.' Generic Lamaholot; Ile Ape and the Lembata dialects (other than Lamalera vowel length) are not discussed.

sources.citation: Krausse, Daniel. 2016. A brief grammar of the Eastern Atadei language of Lembata, Indonesia. Linguistik Indonesia 34(2).
sources.note: Ile Ape named only in the list of Lembata languages ('West Lembata, Ile Ape, Levuka..'); stress remarks concern Eastern Atadei only.

sources.citation: Marolly, Elizabeth Rilyn Marsella, Sebastianus Fernandez, Yosep B. Kroon & Zantty O. Padahana. 2024. A syntactic analysis of the basic sentence patterns in Ile Ape dialect of Lamaholot language. Sintaksis 2(3): 105-121. doi:10.61132/sintaksis.v2i3.890
sources.note: Nothing. Syntax only (five basic sentence patterns); sec. 2.6 gives background (Ile Ape = Nusa Tadon, c. 18,000 speakers, north Lembata near the Ile Ape volcano); examples carry no stress marks; references list no prior Ile Ape phonology.

sources.citation: Nugroho, Zefanya Christiady & Heppy Christinawati Silaen. 2024. Dinamika ketahanan bahasa-bahasa rumpun Lamaholot di Lembata. Linguistik Indonesia 42(1). doi:10.26499/li.v42i1.578
sources.note: Nothing. Participatory vitality survey (Ile Ape surveyed at desa Tokojaeng; vitality revised from Ethnologue 6b to 6a); no phonology.

sources.citation: Klamer, Marian & Francesca R. Moro (eds.). 2023. Traces of Contact in the Lexicon: Austronesian and Papuan Studies. Leiden/Boston: Brill. DOI 10.1163/9789004529458. (incl. ch. 6: Schapper, Antoinette & Juliette Huber, 'Entwined Histories: The Lexicons of Kawaimina and Maka Languages', 180-209; ch. 8: Gerstner-Link, Claudia, 'Multilateral Lexical Transfer among Four Papuan Language Families: Border, Nimboran, Sentani, and Sko', 263-306; ch. 3 Klamer on Timor-Alor-Pantar/Austronesian contact, 57-100; ch. 5 Fricke on Lamaholot, 140-179; ch. 7 Moro, Sulistyono & Kaiping on Alorese, 213-262.)
sources.note: Word forms only ('Lamaholot (Ile Ape) bəənawa "forest"', p252); no phonology.

sources.citation: Silaen, Heppy C. & Renhard Saupia. 2023. Kesalingmengertian dalam rumpun bahasa Lamaholot di Pulau Lembata. Bahasa: Jurnal Keilmuan Pendidikan Bahasa dan Sastra Indonesia 5(2). doi:10.26499/bahasa.v5i2.654
sources.note: Only other recent paper with Ile Ape field data (intelligibility testing); could contain wordlist transcriptions or a phonological note; blocked by an automated-access block here.

sources.citation: Sulistyono, Yunus. 2022. A history of Alorese (Austronesian): combining linguistic and oral history. LOT Dissertation Series 614 (PhD thesis, Leiden University). Amsterdam: LOT. Table 5.2 lists 'Ile Ape | ila | Lembata | Keraf 1978 | 198 [core items]' among the Western Lamaholot varieties compared; sec. 5.5.5.2 discusses Ile Ape reflexes.
sources.note: Nothing on Ile Ape stress. The only stress section (4.2.4.4, p. 90) is Alorese: 'Stress in Alorese is marked by higher pitch. If words are uttered in isolation, such as in a wordlist, stress almost always occurs on the penultimate syllable.' Ile Ape content: 'the PFL final *-m is retained as m only in Ile Ape, but becomes -ŋ in Lewoingu and Lamalera' and 'Ile Ape retains the final -m as shown in the words mitəm "black" and kələm "sky"' (sec. 5.5.5.2); forms carry no stress marks.

sources.citation: Fricke, Hanna L.A. 2019. Traces of language contact: The Flores-Lembata languages in eastern Indonesia. LOT Dissertation Series 544. Utrecht: LOT.
sources.note: Stress section 3.2.5 (p. 49) describes Central Lembata (levu1239) only. Ile Ape appears solely as wordlist lect 'ia' (ISO ila, source Keraf 1978b) in the appendix source table and in comparative word tables (e.g. p. 69); no Ile Ape stress statement.

sources.citation: Kaiping, Gereon A., Owen Edwards & Marian Klamer (eds.). 2019. LexiRumah 3.0.0. Leiden: Leiden University Centre for Linguistics. Lect lama1277-ileap 'Ile Ape Lamaholot' (197 forms, Source keraf1978 = Keraf, Gregorius. 1978. Morfologi Dialek Lamalera, 'Daftar Kata Dasar'; 'coordinates approximated from Keraf map').
sources.note: Bare 197-item basic-vocabulary list in segmental transcription (Form / Local_Orthography / Segments, e.g. kələm 'sky', ləra 'sun', təmala 'star', bərebot = berébot 'lake'); no stress or tone marks anywhere (0 occurrences of ˈ ˌ ' ´); the acute in Local_Orthography (ilé, apé, talé) distinguishes /e/ from schwa <e>, it is not an accent mark. Answers the list of works to obtain question: Keraf's Ile Ape list, as digitized, carries no stress information. Wordlist-only data, not a statement.

sources.citation: Sulistyono, Yunus & Inyo Yos Fernandez. 2019. Linguistic situation around East Flores and Alor-Pantar islands in East Indonesia. Humanities & Social Sciences Reviews 7(3). doi:10.18510/hssr.2019.7329
sources.note: Nothing; Ile Ape is not mentioned.

sources.citation: Kroon, Yosep B. 2016. A grammar of Solor-Lamaholot: A language of Flores, eastern Indonesia. PhD thesis, University of Adelaide.
sources.note: Sec. 3.4 'SL has a fixed stress pattern.. commonly assigned to a penultimate syllable' is Solor Lamaholot only; Ile Ape is not mentioned anywhere in the text.

sources.citation: Robinson, Laura C. 2015. The Alor-Pantar (Papuan) languages and Austronesian contact in East Nusantara. In Malcolm D. Ross & I Wayan Arka (eds.), Language change in Austronesian languages: Papers from 12-ICAL, vol. 3 (Asia-Pacific Linguistics 018), 19-33. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics. hdl:1885/13386.
sources.note: Nothing: Ile Ape appears only as a label on three or four lexical comparanda and in the source table; no transcription carries stress and there is no prosodic remark about any Lamaholot variety.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Ile Ape language' (single reference: Ethnologue 18th ed. 2015)

'dialek Amakala' at Desa Amakaka, Kec. Ile Ape and 'dialek Jontona' at Desa Jontona, Kec. Ile Ape).

sources.note: No phonology content: village list, dialectometric percentages (>81% difference from Kawela, Hewa, Kedang, Sikka) and the 17-dialect inventory only. Useful as a pointer that Badan Bahasa holds first-hand Ile Ape (Amakaka, Jontona) questionnaire data.
